newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Westpac Australia leading index rises in Jan.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Westpac Australia leading index rises in Jan.

text.p: The Westpac-Melbourne Institute leading index of Australian economic activity, which indicates where activity will be in six to nine months time, rose by 1.4 points or 1.0 percent in January, Westpac said on Wednesday.
The coincident index, which measures current economic activity, rose by 3.0 points or 1.7 percent in January.
The leading index of inflation fell 0.2 of one point to 4.2 percent in January, to be at its lowest level since November 1994.

"The strong rise in the leading index in January reinforces the upward trend evident in the previous three months and has pushed the smooth growth rate in the leading index to four percent, its strongest pace since October 1994," Westpac general manager, economic strategy and planning, Bill Evans said.

The strong rise in the coincident index reflected the strength in retail sales and employment in Janaury and tentatively suggested some recovery from the very weak activity in the December, Evans said in a statement.
"The leading index flags a continuing mild recovery in the first half of 1997, with the rising prospect of stronger economic conditions emerging in the second half," he said.
The fall in the leading index pointed to a fall in underlying inflation in the first half of 1997, with Westpac expecting an annual rate of 1.8 percent by mid 1997.
The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) targets the underlying rate, aiming to keep it to an average of between two and three percent over a run of years.

Evans also said there was a strong chance the U.S. Federal Reserve will tighten U.S. monetary policy in the next few months, but said the positive local inflation outlook posed no risk that the RBA would follow suit.
"Indeed, while expecting the economy to improve, Westpac sees little risk of an upswing in the interest rate cycle before mid-1998," he said.
Internationally, Evans said the leading index for all countries was running marginally above trend.
The U.S continued to remain robust, but he said the most encouraging aspect was the positive direction of the leading indicators in Europe and Japan.

"An expected lift in world economic activity in the second half of 1997 and 1998 would be a major boost to Australia both directly and indirectly, via the lift it would give to the East Asian economies," he said.
